analysis.summary:
This 55-year-old male presents with persistent dry cough following an upper respiratory infection, complicated by a 3-cm lung mass for which he has declined surgical intervention. The clinical presentation is that of a mixed deficiency-excess pattern: the lung mass itself represents an accumulation of pathogenic phlegm and blood stasis (the excess component), while the patient's weak constitution, compromised recovery, and depleted reserves indicate underlying Qi and Yin deficiency (the deficiency component). This mixed pattern explains why simple antimicrobial treatment failed to resolve the cough—the illness has progressed beyond acute infection into chronic structural pathology rooted in constitutional weakness.

The tongue findings are diagnostic: enlargement with teeth marks indicates Spleen Qi deficiency and fluid accumulation; the pale-red body (neither fully pale nor fully red) suggests mixed cold and mild heat with overall qi insufficiency; the white coating reveals incompletely resolved phlegm-damp pathology. The sublingual vein distension is a key additional sign of blood stasis—the phlegm and blood are both stagnant, which is characteristic of masses that form through prolonged accumulation in a weak terrain. The deep, thready pulse confirms this narrative: the deep quality locates the disease as interior and structural (hence the imaging findings of the mass), while the thready quality reveals the qi and blood deficiency that allowed the pathogenic accumulation in the first place.

The patient's choice to decline surgery shifts the role of TCM from adjunctive post-operative support to primary non-surgical management aimed at stabilizing the mass, reducing symptom severity, and slowing or preventing progression. At age 55 with constitutional Qi deficiency, this patient's body has limited capacity to spontaneously reabsorb the mass; instead, the therapeutic goal is to strengthen Lung qi and yin (to improve local immune defense and tissue repair), tonify Spleen qi (to halt further fluid accumulation and improve overall constitution), and gently resolve the stagnant phlegm and blood without provoking hemorrhage or rapid shift in the mass's properties.

Critically, this diagnosis assumes that the 3-cm lung mass has been definitively identified as a benign or low-grade lesion suitable for conservative management. If imaging suggests malignancy or rapid growth, the management paradigm changes entirely. Moreover, TCM's role here is explicitly complementary: imaging surveillance every 3-6 months is mandatory, and any change in cough character, appearance of hemoptysis, weight loss, or acute dyspnea requires immediate medical re-evaluation. The patient must understand that while TCM can strengthen constitution and reduce symptom burden, it is not curative for structural masses and is no substitute for conventional oncologic monitoring.

key_findings.from_pulse: Deep pulse (interior location of disease, structural pathology); thready pulse (Qi and Yin deficiency, weak vessel tone from depletion). Combined deep + thready is highly specific for deficiency with interior pathology—not acute exterior, not pure heat, not simple blood deficiency.
key_findings.from_other: Age 55 places patient in early senescence when constitutional yin naturally declines; history of upper respiratory infection is the identifiable trigger but only succeeded because of pre-existing Qi insufficiency; the fact that a 3-cm mass formed suggests either the infection was severe or the underlying constitution was seriously weakened; imaging findings (3-cm lung mass) are the objective structural pathology that TCM must address within its framework.

analysis.pattern_rationale: The diagnosis of Lung Qi and Yin Deficiency with Phlegm Obstruction and Blood Stasis is supported by converging evidence across all four examinations. First, inquiry: The dry cough is a classic Lung Yin deficiency symptom (loss of body fluids, inability to moisten the airways), while its persistence despite the acute infection resolving indicates a chronic deficiency state rather than lingering pathogen. The shortness of breath combined with a physical mass suggests both Qi deficiency (weak qi cannot move air efficiently) and mechanical obstruction (phlegm-mass blocks airways). The post-URI timing and patient's failure to fully recover point to Spleen Qi deficiency impairing the clearance of residual pathogenic phlegm. Second, tongue: The enlarged body with teeth marks is pathognomonic for Spleen Qi deficiency (inability to move and transform fluids, leading to fluid retention that pushes the tongue against the teeth). The pale-red color (not crimson red) argues against full-blown Heat and instead suggests a cooling, qi-deficient terrain with some residual pathogenic qi (hence not purely pale). The white coating (not thick-yellow) indicates cold-damp or incompletely resolved pathogenic fluids, not inflammatory heat. Together, these tongue signs point to Spleen Qi deficiency as the foundation and Lung Yin deficiency as the activated pathology. Third, pulse: The deep quality locates the pathology in the interior (consistent with a 3-cm structural mass in the lungs, not a superficial acute illness). The thready quality reveals depleted Qi and Blood; a strong, wiry, or slippery pulse would suggest excess, but a thready pulse in a 55-year-old with chronic illness and a mass indicates constitutional weakness. The combination of deep + thready is seen in deficiency with interior pathology, not in excess. Fourth, structural evidence: The 3-cm lung mass itself, while appearing as 'excess' (an accumulation), can only have formed because of prolonged stagnation in a weakened terrain. In TCM pathophysiology, tumors and masses are understood as the end result of qi deficiency allowing phlegm and blood to accumulate locally. Therefore, the mass is the 'manifest excess' but the 'root is deficiency.' Fifth, age and history: At age 55, the patient is entering a period of natural constitutional yin decline. The upper respiratory infection was the trigger, but his inability to fully recover and the subsequent crystallization of a mass indicate that underlying Qi and Yin reserves were already exhausted. This matches the Qi-deficient constitution type. Secondary Pattern: Spleen Qi Deficiency is listed as secondary because, while it is a foundational weakness, the active pathology is in the Lung. However, the secondary pattern is clinically relevant because strengthening the Spleen will improve fluid transformation and help prevent further accumulation.

treatment.therapeutic_principle: Tonify Lung Qi and Yin to restore function and local immunity; Fortify Spleen Qi to halt fluid accumulation and support constitutional recovery; Gently soften hardness and disperse accumulation (phlegm and blood stasis) without aggressive circulation promotion that could destabilize the mass.
treatment.treatment_method: Primary approach: Use tonifying herbs to supplement Lung and Spleen Qi as the foundation, paired with mild Yin-nourishing herbs to sustain the Lungs' moistening and cooling functions. Secondary approach: Add gentle phlegm-resolving and mild blood-moving herbs (such as Salvia miltiorrhiza, which moves blood but is not heating) to slowly disperse the stagnant phlegm and blood underlying the mass, without causing hemorrhage or acute symptom flare. Tertiary approach: Support Kidney yin as the long-term reserve, especially important at age 55 when natural yin is declining. Sequencing: Begin with tonification as the primary action (3-4 weeks), then gradually introduce mild softening herbs once the Qi foundation is stronger (weeks 5-8+). Avoid aggressive heat or aggressive blood-movers that could cause bleeding from the mass. Treatment duration is likely 3-6 months minimum to show measurable changes in cough and potentially in imaging; patient must maintain concurrent medical imaging surveillance.

recipes: Ginseng and Lily Bulb Porridge: Cook 1 bowl rice with 6g dried ginseng, 15g dried lily bulb, and 3-4 pieces of goji. Simmer for 1 hour until thick. Eat warm, once daily in the morning. Purpose: tonifies Lung and Spleen qi, nourishes yin, gradually improves cough and energy.

Tremella and Pear Dessert Soup: Soak 5-6g dried tremella overnight, clean and shred. Stew with 1 fresh pear (cored and cubed), 10 red dates (pitted), and 2 cups of water for 45 minutes. Add honey to taste. Eat warm 2-3 times per week. Purpose: moistens Lung yin, soothes dry cough, nourishes skin and fluid reserves without creating heat or heaviness.

foods_to_avoid: Smoking and secondhand smoke / smoky foods — directly irritates Lung tissue, worsens cough, and promotes cancer risk; absolute contraindication for this patient
Deep-fried and greasy foods (fried chicken, fatty pork, oil-rich pastries) — create phlegm and damp-heat, directly opposing Spleen's fluid transformation, promoting further mass accumulation
Spicy and pungent foods (chili, garlic, raw onion) — can irritate the Lung cough reflex, promote inflammation around the mass, deplete yin fluids further through sweating
lifestyle: Maintain consistent sleep schedule with 7-8 hours per night, especially before 11 PM — Yin recovery occurs during sleep, and lung yin depletion requires adequate rest to regenerate; disrupted sleep worsens dry cough and delays healing

Avoid air pollution, secondhand smoke, and chemical exposures — direct irritation to the Lungs; if living in a polluted area, use an air purifier with HEPA filter and N95 mask during high-pollution days

Maintain adequate humidity in the living environment (40-60% relative humidity) using a humidifier, especially in winter or dry climates — moistens the airways, reduces cough irritation, and supports Lung yin function

Practice gentle movement such as tai chi, slow walking, or qigong for 20-30 minutes daily at a relaxed pace — strengthens qi circulation without depleting yin reserves; avoid strenuous exercise which can exhaust qi and worsen breathlessness
acupoints: Lung 9 (located at the wrist crease, in the thumb-side depression just lateral to the radial artery) — Massage with firm thumb pressure in circular motions for 1-2 minutes, 2-3 times daily. This is the tonification point of the Lung channel; it directly tonifies Lung Qi and Yin, and is foundational for any Lung condition. Essential for restoring Lung function and reducing dry cough.

Spleen 6 (located on the inner lower leg, 3 finger-widths above the highest point of the ankle bone, slightly posterior to the tibia) — Massage with firm thumb pressure in circular motions for 1-2 minutes, 1-2 times daily. This point tonifies Spleen, nourishes yin, and regulates fluid distribution; critical for addressing the Spleen Qi deficiency and phlegm accumulation.

Stomach 36 (located on the outer lower leg, 3 finger-widths below the kneecap depression, one finger-width lateral to the anterior tibial crest/shin bone) — Massage with firm thumb pressure in circular motions for 1-2 minutes, 1-2 times daily, or apply warm moxibustion (warm moxa stick held 2 inches above) for 5-10 minutes daily. This is the premier immune support point; tonifies qi generally, strengthens the Spleen, and enhances constitutional resilience against disease progression.
exercise: Tai Chi or Qigong: Practice a gentle form (8-form or 13-form Tai Chi, or basic Qigong) for 20-30 minutes daily, ideally in the early morning or early evening. Tai Chi strengthens qi circulation, preserves yin by avoiding excessive sweating, and improves both balance and immune function; particularly valuable for Qi-deficient constitutions. Avoid competitive sports or high-intensity exercise.

Walking (slow, mindful pace): Walk at a comfortable pace for 30 minutes, 4-5 times per week, in a park or quiet area with fresh air (avoiding pollution). This maintains cardiovascular function, strengthens the Lungs through gentle breathing, and does not deplete qi stores like running would.
recommendations.emotional_care: At age 55 with a known lung mass, the patient is likely experiencing existential anxiety, fear of progression or mortality, and possibly grief over the lost option of aggressive treatment. TCM recognizes that the Lungs house the corporeal soul and govern grief and attachment to loss. To support emotional wellness: (1) Practice acceptance-based meditation or cognitive-behavioral techniques to process fear and reduce rumination, which depletes Qi. (2) Engage in meaningful activities and maintain social connections, as isolation worsens Qi stagnation. (3) Consider whether the decision to decline surgery involved closure or unresolved conflict—unfinished emotional business impairs healing and should be addressed with family or a therapist. (4) Use the daily acupressure ritual (especially Lung 9, Spleen 6, Stomach 36) as a mindfulness practice, bringing awareness and care to the Lungs during the massage. (5) Avoid becoming obsessive about imaging results and symptom tracking, which feeds anxiety; instead, establish a fixed schedule for medical follow-up and trust the process between appointments. (6) If depression or persistent anxiety develops, seek professional mental health support concurrent with TCM—emotional and physical health are inseparable in TCM philosophy.

warning_signs: Increase in cough frequency or severity, or change in cough character (e.g., from dry to wet) — may indicate progression of the mass or secondary infection; requires immediate imaging and medical evaluation
Hemoptysis (coughing up blood or blood-tinged sputum) — sign of mass erosion or bleeding into airway; medical emergency, requires immediate hospital evaluation and imaging
Chest pain or pleuritic pain (sharp pain worse with breathing) — may indicate mass involving the pleura or pericardium; requires urgent medical assessment
Worsening shortness of breath at rest or new symptoms of wheezing — may indicate airway obstruction from mass growth or fluid accumulation; requires same-day medical evaluation
Unexplained weight loss of more than 5-10 pounds over 1-2 months — concerning for metabolic changes or disease progression; requires medical evaluation
Persistent high fever (above 38.5°C / 101.3°F) lasting more than 3-5 days — suggests infection or systemic inflammation; requires medical assessment

New symptoms such as hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement), facial swelling (superior vena cava syndrome), or neurological symptoms — red flags for mass expansion into adjacent structures; immediate imaging and medical evaluation required
contraindications: Absolutely no smoking or use of tobacco products in any form — directly damages Lungs, accelerates mass growth risk, and worsens cough

Avoid aggressive blood-moving or warming herbs (such as Tao Ren, Hong Hua, raw ginger, cinnamon bark in large doses, or Angelica sinensis in large amounts) — risk of bleeding from or around the mass; only gentle blood movers in small amounts under practitioner supervision
Do not use herbs known to promote rapid Qi circulation without medical supervision — carry risk of destabilizing the mass or causing hemorrhage

Avoid high-dose Ginseng without monitoring — while mild tonification is beneficial, excessive heating can promote inflammation around the mass; keep doses moderate (6-12g/day decoction, not mega-doses)
Avoid intense or competitive physical exercise — depletes qi reserves and can precipitate acute symptoms
Do not delay or skip scheduled medical imaging and oncology follow-ups in favor of TCM treatment alone — TCM is complementary, not a substitute for conventional imaging surveillance
precautions.special_notes: CRITICAL CONTEXT: This patient has a 3-cm lung mass of uncertain behavior (benign vs. malignant, slow-growing vs. aggressive). While TCM can support symptom management, immune function, and quality of life, it CANNOT cure or reliably shrink a lung mass. (1) IMAGING SURVEILLANCE IS MANDATORY: The patient MUST undergo repeat chest imaging (CT or X-ray) every 3-6 months to monitor the mass's size, appearance, and any signs of progression. This is not optional—it is the safety net for detecting dangerous change that TCM alone cannot manage. (2) SPECIALIST CONSULTATION: If the mass has not been characterized by an oncologist or pulmonologist, the patient should be encouraged to seek one consultation to confirm that conservative management is truly appropriate (e.g., the mass is likely benign or slow-growing, not aggressive cancer). (3) RED FLAG MONITORING: Because cough and shortness of breath are common in both Lung Qi deficiency AND mass progression, the patient must be trained to recognize the red-flag symptoms and seek medical care immediately if they occur. (4) HERBAL-DRUG INTERACTIONS: If the patient is taking any conventional medications (including chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy if the mass is later determined to be malignant), a licensed herbalist MUST review the herbal formula for interactions before starting. Some tonifying herbs can interfere with certain cancer therapies. (5) AGE AND CONSTITUTION: At age 55 with Qi-deficient constitution and a structural lung mass, the prognosis depends heavily on early detection of progression. Slow-growing benign lesions may remain stable for years with conservative care; malignant lesions progress rapidly and require aggressive intervention. TCM's role is to support the former scenario while being vigilant for the latter. (6) DURATION OF CARE: Expect that supportive TCM care for this condition will be long-term (many months to years) rather than short-term. The goal is stabilization and symptom relief, not cure.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess TCM progress at 3-4 weeks after starting herbal formulas and lifestyle modifications. At this point, the patient should report whether cough frequency has decreased, energy has improved, and sleep quality has improved. If yes, continue the same regimen for another 4-8 weeks. If no improvement or worsening, adjust the herbal formula (consult a TCM practitioner) or investigate for possible complications requiring medical evaluation. Conventional medical imaging (chest X-ray or CT scan) should be performed every 3-6 months on a fixed schedule regardless of TCM progress. Do not allow TCM improvement in symptoms to delay or cancel scheduled imaging—symptom improvement and imaging stability must both be confirmed.
follow_up.expected_improvement: By week 4: Reduced cough frequency (fewer episodes per day), improved sleep quality (able to sleep through the night or with fewer night-time coughs), improved appetite, and increased energy levels. By week 8: Cough becomes less dry (more moist or mucoid, indicating yin restoration and phlegm beginning to mobilize), reduced shortness of breath with mild exertion, improved sense of well-being. By 12 weeks: Significant reduction in cough (possibly fewer than 5 episodes per day versus baseline), improved exercise tolerance, improved energy. IMAGING LEVEL: Ideally, the 3-cm lung mass remains stable in size on imaging at 3-6 months (no growth is the goal; actual shrinkage is less common in benign lesions but possible with slow response to qi tonification). If imaging shows growth, the patient MUST be referred back to oncology for reassessment of treatment options.
follow_up.next_steps: (1) Schedule repeat chest imaging at 3 months if not already scheduled; confirm with primary physician or pulmonologist that a surveillance schedule is in place. (2) Continue daily acupressure self-care (Lung 9, Spleen 6, Stomach 36) for at least 6 months, ideally ongoing. (3) Maintain dietary modifications and lifestyle guidelines (sleep, humidity, stress management) as permanent habits. (4) At week 4 reassessment, decide with the TCM practitioner whether to continue the first herbal formula or rotate to the second or add gentle blood-moving components (week 5+ onward). Do not stop herbal care abruptly; taper gradually if discontinuing. (5) If the patient develops any red-flag symptoms, seek medical evaluation immediately; do not rely on TCM alone to manage acute complications. (6) If imaging at 3-6 months shows mass growth or concerning changes, revisit the original decision not to pursue surgery or other conventional therapies; growth changes the risk-benefit calculation.
